title: Japanese Drifter’s Road Trip to Korea Drives Uchiyama Takuya’s ‘The Blue Breaks’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: A man conceived through sperm donation, unsure of his place in the world, sets out on a journey to Korea in “The Blue Breaks,” an adaptation of Mac
body:
A man conceived through sperm donation, unsure of his place in the world, sets out on a journey to Korea in “The Blue Breaks,” an adaptation of Machiya Ryohei’s 2016 novel by Japanese filmmaker Uchiyama Takuya (“Numb”). The Japan-Italy co-production was among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	The protagonist, Shukichi, is a rootless part-time worker in his thirties living at Japan’s western edge. His sense of detachment grows when he discovers that his girlfriend, with whom he lives, has a son she no longer has custody of. A night spent with a solitary boxer of Korean descent then throws his sense of identity and sexuality into further confusion.
	

	He later meets Toko, a young woman who is terminally ill but carries herself lightly, smoking and smiling despite the little time she has left. Her outlook gradually leaves its mark on him. Eventually Shukichi and the people around him travel to Korea together, where they reckon with one another’s lives and deaths.

	Uchiyama, who has previously written his own screenplays from personal experience, said he felt drawn to the book in part because it was published in the year he started making films, and because Machiya wrote it at the age Uchiyama is now.

	“Shukichi, the protagonist, struggles with the part of himself that never quite became ‘manly.’ I’ve also spent much of my life feeling uncomfortable with what society expects a man to be,” Uchiyama said.

	He described the characters as people whose lives look very different from one another’s, and said Japan still expects everyone to be alike.
	

	“Diversity isn’t something new. It’s always been there, even if we haven’t always acknowledged it,” Uchiyama said. “I wanted to approach these feelings with a sense of lightness, and to make a film about love that is unapologetically romantic.”

	Japanese producer Satoh Naomi of Differentia is behind the project, with Parsifal Reparato of Italian company Antropica as co-producer. The team is working on the screenplay, casting and financing, with a shoot planned for 2027 and completion in 2028, and is targeting a premiere at an international festival.

	Satoh said the two connected over a shared sense of not fitting the roles expected of them, whether in society at large or within the film business, and that films that resist categories can be hard to finance in Japan.

	“When ‘Numb’ was selected for the Berlinale, it gave me real proof that Takuya’s work could resonate with audiences beyond Japan,” Satoh said.

	In Tokyo, the producers made headway on the remaining financing and find international co-production partners, sales agents and distributors who could take the film beyond Japan and Italy.

	Reparato said the film’s appeal lies in how it rethinks family and identity, and that Antropica, which has been active in Asia for years, including in Vietnam, sees the project as a way to deepen ties with Japanese cinema, helped by Italy and Japan’s bilateral co-production framework.

	“At this historical moment, building bridges is more important than ever,” Reparato said.

	Uchiyama has also wrapped shooting on a separate project, which is now moving into editing.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market ran as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Japanese Drifter’s Road Trip to Korea Drives Uchiyama Takuya’s ‘The Blue Breaks’ at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: Korea Box Office: Anime Hit ‘Chiikawa’ Retains Lead as Brad Pitt Thriller ‘Heart of the Beast’ Debuts
description: Japanese animated phenomenon “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” held the No. 1 position at the South Korean box office over the
body:
Japanese animated phenomenon “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” held the No. 1 position at the South Korean box office over the weekend of Oct. 30–Nov. 1, securing its third consecutive weekend atop the rankings. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Toho-distributed fantasy release generated $1.7 million from 221,651 admissions across 1,167 screens, claiming 32.1% of the weekend market. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the popular manga by Nagano, the animated blockbuster has reached a cumulative gross of $20.1 million from 2,583,851 total admissions since its Sep. 30 rollout.
	

	Sony Pictures and TriStar’s survival thriller “Heart of the Beast” opened in second place, pulling in $1.2 million from 162,790 admissions across 1,106 screens to capture 23% of theatrical revenue. Since opening mid-week on Oct. 28, the title has accumulated $1.5 million from 215,237 admissions.

	By4M Studio and Barunson E&A’s workplace comedy “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng” debuted in third place, taking in $326,609 from 44,799 admissions across 677 screens for 6.09% of the market. The directorial debut of screenwriter Lee Yong-jae stars Lee Sun-bin, Yoo Jae-myung, Kim Young-min, and Jeon Seok-ho, following a high school language teacher unexpectedly sequestered into the top-secret 40-day test-writing committee for the national college entrance examination. Following its premiere at the Busan International Film Festival and an Oct. 28 commercial bow, the comedy has grossed $505,208 from 71,767 viewers.
	

	Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” placed fourth in its sixth frame, collecting $307,719 from 41,265 admissions across 620 screens for 5.7% of receipts. Distributed by Hive Media Corp and starring Yu Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho, the drama reconstructs the August 15, 1974 assassination attempt on President Park Chung-hee. Despite ongoing legal complaints and protests from conservative civic groups alleging historical distortion over its portrayal of state inquiry contradictions, the title lifted its cumulative total to $25.5 million from 3,448,036 admissions since its Sep. 23 launch.

	Anime re-release “Attack on Titan: Crimson Arrows” placed fifth, grossing $266,616 from 30,263 admissions across 233 screens. The theatrical re-issue of the 2014 feature pushed its updated cumulative haul to $547,187 from 72,324 admissions.

	CJ ENM’s gambling drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” took sixth place, earning $208,310 from 26,650 admissions across 498 screens. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the comic-adapted franchise officially crossed the two-million-ticket threshold, reaching $15.7 million from 2,055,522 total viewers.

	CJ Entertainment’s psychological thriller “Paradise Lost,” directed by Yeon Sang-ho and starring Kim Hyun-joo and Bae Hyun-sung, placed seventh on the admissions chart with $124,104 from 17,053 admissions across 593 screens, bringing its cume to $1 million from 151,429 admissions.

	Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” placed eighth in admissions with 16,641 viewers across 444 screens, though it generated a higher revenue gross of $140,321. The film has accumulated $899,915 from 115,464 admissions.

	Universal’s tentpole “The Odyssey” took ninth place in its 13th weekend, adding $108,833 from 13,332 admissions across 254 screens. The film took 2.02% of the frame, lifting its cumulative total to $106.4 million from 12,335,377 admissions since its Aug. 5 opening.

	Rounding out the top ten, Japanese romantic drama “You, Like a Star” debuted with $77,264 from 10,091 admissions across 154 screens. Directed by Michihito Fujii and starring Ryusei Yokohama and Suzu Hirose as young lovers bound by shared hardship on an island in the Seto Inland Sea, the film has grossed $146,509 from 20,478 admissions since its Oct. 28 release.
	

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $5.3 million, down from last week’s $5.6 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: Anime Hit ‘Chiikawa’ Retains Lead as Brad Pitt Thriller ‘Heart of the Beast’ Debuts

title: ‘Criminal Minds: Evolution’ Stars A.J. Cook, Paget Brewster and More React to Series Cancellation: ‘Rest in Peace’
description: Following the news that “Criminal Minds: Evolution” has been canceled at Paramount+, stars A.J. Cook, Paget Brewster, Kirsten Vangsness and more ar
body:
Following the news that “Criminal Minds: Evolution” has been canceled at Paramount+, stars A.J. Cook, Paget Brewster, Kirsten Vangsness and more are looking back on the crime drama’s 20 Season run.

	The announcement seems to have come at the perfect time to mourn a TV show, as Cook chose to mark the end of this installment of “Criminal Minds” with a photo of her dressed up for Halloween, wearing a tombstone for Jennifer Jareau, the special agent who she’s played since “Criminal Minds” debuted in 2005. (Jareau, also known as JJ, was the BAU’s media/police liaison before becoming a profiler in later seasons.) She captioned the snap, “Rest in peace JJ (for now) #criminalminds #halloween #stillprocessing.”
	

	Brewster, who played FBI supervisory special agent Emily Prentiss since “Criminal Minds” Season 2, shared a black-and-white photo with the text “Free Agent.” RJ Hatanaka also kept his tribute short and sweet, sharing a photo of the cast with the caption, “Just the finest group of people.” Hatanaka, who played FBI agent Tyler Green, joined the show in Season 16.

	“Social media is sort of like getting to do your own press conference I guess. This has happened. It’s being canceled, but then it says right there it’s ending ‘for now,’” said Vangsness in a video shared on Instagram. The actress, who played Penelope Garcia, a technical analyst beloved in part for her relationship with agent Derek Morgan (Shemar Moore) during the show’s original run, has portrayed the character since Season 1.

	She continued: “You know the part in ‘Charlie and the Chocolate Factory’ where Charlie gets the chocolate, and it’s a little bittersweet. He’s like, ‘Thank you so much for the chocolate.’ Look at how long, that doesn’t happen ever,’” she continued, referencing the show’s 20 Season run. “But I love my job, and my boss Erica Messer says there are so many more stories to tell. So if we get to keep telling them somewhere, that would be amazing. I know all of us feel the same way.”
	

	In the video caption, she wrote that her “heart fireworks in appreciation for the time at this job @criminalminds and my co-horts at fake murder camp @pagetpagetgram @ajcook @aishatyler @rjhatanaka @adamrodriguez @joemantegna.”

	News first broke that the long-running procedural would end with its 20th season on Friday. “Evolution,” which picks up after the events of the original “Criminal Minds,” was originally revived for Season 16 back in 2022, and continued the show after it was renewed for a fifteenth and final season at CBS in Jan. 2019. Season 19 aired between May and July earlier this year. Season 20 will air in 2027.

	“Evolution” also stars Joe Mantegna, Aisha Tyler and Adam Rodriguez.

schema.headline: ‘Criminal Minds: Evolution’ Stars A.J. Cook, Paget Brewster and More React to Series Cancellation: ‘Rest in Peace’

title: Five Takeaways From Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s Largest Comic-Con: ‘Harry Potter’ and ‘Percy Jackson’ Fandoms Are Alive and Well, As Are Cosplayers
description:
Over the last few days, Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s largest Comic-Con, has been celebrating its 60th anniversary.

	The medieval city located
body:
Over the last few days, Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s largest Comic-Con, has been celebrating its 60th anniversary.

	The medieval city located in Italy’s Tuscany region hosted creative leaders, artists and players of games, authors of comic books, manga, showrunners and animators of TV series and anime, actors and directors of films. Around 80,000 ticket-paying fans per day flooded the city and visited the various pavilions, exhibitions and pop-up experiences dotted throughout the city.
	

	Here are five takeaways from this year’s event.

	Queues for HBO’s Harry Potter pavilion began in the early morning before crocodiling and winding around the pavilion. Visitors were treated to a peek at props from the show, were given temporary tattoos for the House of their choice and got to see a specially filmed message from John Lithgow and Nick Frost, who play Albus Dumbledore and Hagrid respectively. Given the obvious anticipation of the show, it was a pity that no one from the show was physically present nor were there any previews of footage granted. Many of the fans were cautious in their enthusiasm. A fan of the films, Stefano – who was confusingly dressed as a Jedi – told Variety, “It will be fun to see the books addressed in a way that is deeper.” Alessia, from Lake Como and dressed as Maleficent, worried that “they’ve made too many changes.” Perhaps, the showmakers were worried about such doubts being expressed prior to the show’s release on Christmas Day.

	“Percy Jackson and the Olympians” fandom is alive and well, and turned up with a large presence including key cast members Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries and Aryan Simhadri as well as showrunners Jonathan E. Steinberg and Dan Shotz. Having attended a panel earlier in the day, the cast appeared on a terrace overlooking Piazza della Magione to greet over 8000 fans who had gathered dressed in the colors of Camp Halfblood from the show.
	

	The live-action adaptation of the “Blue Lock” anime and manga series received a European premiere. The film follows an authoritarian regime who have set up a kind of survival game to choose the most selfish (and therefore best) soccer striker from 300 candidates, with the ultimate aim of winning Japan the World Cup. The film is a faithful rendering of its anime predecessor and plays like a demented mix of “Battle Royale” and the Michael Caine soccer pic “Victory.”

	The return of Frank Miller (“The Dark Knight Returns,” “Sin City”) meant that comic book royalty continues to show up to greet the fans and announce new works. This time a further collaboration with Peach Momoko, which will explore and be inspired by Japanese horror stories. Also, groundbreaking Japanese manga artist Go Nagai was also feted with a special exhibition entitled “Sun, Heart, and Steel,” featuring his groundbreaking “Mazinger Z,” which inaugurated the Mecha genre, as well as his Devilman, which fittingly enough was inspired by the illustration of Dante’s “Divine Comedy.”

	One of the major attractions of Lucca is that provided by the public itself. The dedication and imagination and sheer extravagance of the cosplayers provides the city with a constant rolling panorama of personalities. From the inhabitants of Middle Earth and Hogwarts, to the Mario Bros. and Squid Game, Lucca for a few days becomes a Cosplay Utopia. Spotted among the crowds was “Leon: the Professional” from the 1994 Luc Besson film, complete with silenced pistol and houseplant, a Walter White, a bunch of friends who had come dressed as the cast of the original “Jurassic Park” complete with Jeep. The regular “Star Wars” parade was led by a Mandalorian, who revealed himself to be popular Italian author and television personality Alberto Angela who had spent the day moving through the crowd incognito.

	Lucca Comics and Games ran from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1.

schema.headline: Five Takeaways From Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s Largest Comic-Con: ‘Harry Potter’ and ‘Percy Jackson’ Fandoms Are Alive and Well, As Are Cosplayers

title: Hilary Duff Says She Was ‘F—ing Done’ With ‘Lizzie McGuire’ When It Ended and Never Wanted to Sing ‘What Dreams Are Made Of’ Again: I Was ‘Exhausted By It’
description: Hilary Duff is reflecting on being so “done” playing Lizzie McGuire after the 2003 movie concluded the two-season Disney Channel show that made her
body:
Hilary Duff is reflecting on being so “done” playing Lizzie McGuire after the 2003 movie concluded the two-season Disney Channel show that made her a star. 

	“The Lizzie McGuire Movie” features the now-iconic “What Dreams Are Made Of,” which Duff re-recorded for her 2026 “(Mine)” EP and sang live for the first time on the “Small Rooms, Big Nerves” Tour this year.

	“I was pretty done with Lizzie at that time,” Duff said in a recent interview with Paper magazine about filming the movie. “I had filmed 30 episodes one year and 35 episodes the next. I turned into a huge star. Everyone called me Lizzie. And then I went to Italy to film that movie, and I think I was just like, ‘I’m fucking done with you.’ I want people to see me. This isn’t fun anymore.”
	

	“So now when I sing it, it feels so much better, and I get to join the celebration of what it meant to people, and what it means to me now,” she continued. “I don’t want to sound ungrateful for doing it, but at the time, I was pretty exhausted by it. I was trying to create Hilary Duff separate from Lizzie, so that was right at the midway point where I was like, ‘I’m never singing that song.’ And I didn’t even own it. It wasn’t my song to sing. But now I feel like it is.”

	Duff’s “(Mine)” EP features seven newly re-recorded versions of her greatest hits, originally featured as bonus tracks on vinyl variants of her “Luck… or Something” album.

	“When I look back at that, I’m like, oh my god, I would love a redo,” she said. “All of it was just so crazy. I’m so glad it resonated with people this many years later, and that they loved it and ate it up. But when I perform it now, I’m like, ‘Oh, I’m in this.’ Back then, I just feel like I wasn’t in my body yet.”
	

	Duff starred as Lizzie McGuire on the show, which debuted in January 2001 and also starred Lalaine, Adam Lamberg, Jake Thomas, Hallie Todd and Robert Carradine. The show ended in 2004 with a total of 65 episodes, plus the film.

schema.headline: Hilary Duff Says She Was ‘F—ing Done’ With ‘Lizzie McGuire’ When It Ended and Never Wanted to Sing ‘What Dreams Are Made Of’ Again: I Was ‘Exhausted By It’

title: My Chemical Romance Scores First-Ever No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘The Black Parade,’ 20 Years After Its Release
description: My Chemical Romance has scored its first-ever No. 1 on the Billboard 200 as “The Black Parade” surges from No. 139 to the top of the chart, 20 year
body:
My Chemical Romance has scored its first-ever No. 1 on the Billboard 200 as “The Black Parade” surges from No. 139 to the top of the chart, 20 years after its initial release.

	The group reaches the chart summit for the first time following a deluxe reissue of the album with 78,000 equivalent album units. My Chemical Romance first dropped the album on October 23, 2006, peaking at No. 2 and becoming their highest-charting album until now. With their latest achievement, the band has had the longest-ever wait for an album to return to No. 1, surpassing the near 16-year wait for Toby Keith’s “35 Biggest Hits” following his death in 2024. It also becomes the first anniversary album ever to debut at No. 1.
	

	My Chemical Romance celebrated the 20th anniversary of “The Black Parade” with a five-night series of epic shows at Los Angeles’ Hollywood Bowl, where they performed the album in its entirety and built out its fabled world on the stage. At the time of its release, the sprawling rock opera, which included the hits “Welcome to the Black Parade” and “Teenagers,” was a critically heralded step forward for the quartet, expanding the scope and ambition of their previous work.

	Elsewhere on the Billboard 200, Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” falls from No. 1 to 2, followed by Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem,” Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” and Noah Kahan’s “The Great Divide.” Rounding out Nos. 6 through 10 are Taylor Swift’s “The Life of a Showgirl,” Zach Bryan’s “Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs,” Kahan’s “Stick Season,” Drake’s “Habibti” and Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving.”

schema.headline: My Chemical Romance Scores First-Ever No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘The Black Parade,’ 20 Years After Its Release

title: ‘Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames’ Director and Producer Discuss Bringing the Cult Anime to the Big Screen
description: “Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames” – the latest iteration of the “Gintama” story – previewed this week at Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s largest Comi
body:
“Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames” – the latest iteration of the “Gintama” story – previewed this week at Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s largest Comic-Con, prior to a theatrical release in Italy. Variety spoke with director Naoya Andô and producer Ryo Nakamuray about their continuation of the saga.

	“Gintama” started life as a manga, authored and drawn by Hideaki Sorachi. Set in an alternative, sci-fi version of late-Edo-period Tokyo, the Earth has been invaded by the Amanto, an alien species, and three friends set off on a personal mission.
	

	The manga became a long-running 367-episode anime series and has had three previous big-screen spin-offs. “Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames” is the fourth cinema outing for the series.

	How did you want to approach this franchise without losing its soul but at the same time making it suitably cinematic?Naoya Andô: When we started planning this film, we already knew that there would be many action scenes. We were keen to use the CinemaScope ultrawide ratio as well as using 3D in order to be able to move the camera more, and give us more variety, as well as keep the camera a little distant from the subjects so we could frame the shots better and really appreciate the design and setting. It’s for this reason we made this choice.

	This story was already told in the TV series but despite the title Yoshiwara didn’t burn. But here we see it burn really.Naoya Andô: Our producer Takashi Maekawa also worked on the television series and so I asked him, are we going to actually burn the town this time? And the producer said: “Yes this time we’re going to burn everything.” And so we had talked among ourselves about how we were going to do it and the group made a creative decision to do it.
	

	How important is Lucca Comic and Games for you to reach European fans and markets?Naoya Andô: Obviously, I am very honored and happy to have been invited to such an important event as Lucca. Up til now, we haven’t brought the films to Europe. This time we decided to try and bring the film here. Yesterday, we saw how the Italian fans of “Gintama” love the series and we were very happy to see the warmth of the reception we got.

	Returning to such a well-loved narrative arc as “Yoshiwara in Flames,” how did you deal with the high expectations that audiences would have?Ryo Nakamuray: As you say, even in the original manga, this arc was hugely popular as well as the anime, but we felt there was enough time and we had the benefit of working on a different scale as well.

	How do you transfer from television to the big screen?Naoya Andô: Obviously we tried to find aspects that were big and impressive both in the audio and visual aspects. But we finished the anime five years prior to beginning the film and in these five years, the technology has made great leaps forward. So we wanted to use these new technologies to push the film in new directions, especially using the 3D in the animation. We also worked on the music as well. There is a lot of new music.

	There was a version of the film released earlier this year in Japan and then a new version released in September with over a hundred changed shots. What was behind this decision?Naoya Andô: We released the version in February because we had a deadline to respect and the film was finished and ready to be released, but we also knew that there were shots which weren’t perfect and could be improved and so when we had the opportunity we went back and perfected them. We were very proud of the film we released in February but with the opportunity of the DVD release we decided to go back and work again on the film and we retouched over 200 shots.

	In the end titles there are tens of studios which appear from China to Indonesia to Vietnam. How do you coordinate so many teams?Ryo Nakamuray: In animation, you’re always dividing elements into teams. Some will be experts in character, over action scenes, etc., so we are always choosing the collaborators and animators who will be best for each element and so we’re always meeting up with these different studios and groups. Every group will have a team leader who is responsible for their work.
	

	The film also has quite a lot of humor and meta-humor.Naoya Andô: Humor is very difficult to do and especially to translate culturally. It’s very, very difficult to do. We had one director who worked principally on that. What we figured out was that it was best not to present the humor to the audience as this bit is really funny, but rather have the characters themselves joke between themselves and the audience could listen in and enjoy the humor.

schema.headline: ‘Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames’ Director and Producer Discuss Bringing the Cult Anime to the Big Screen

title: Oscar-Nominated Director James Longley Talks His Afghanistan Documentary ‘Mohabat’ and Why His Next Film Will Center on the Rohingya Genocide (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Double Oscar nominee James Longley, who won the top award at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival on Saturday with “Mohabat,” will focus next on the
body:
Double Oscar nominee James Longley, who won the top award at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival on Saturday with “Mohabat,” will focus next on the Rohingya genocide. 

	Longley – who was Oscar nominated for “Iraq in Fragments” and “Sari’s Mother” – tells Variety at the Czech event, “I’ve already filmed act one of this project, working with Diane Weyermann [who died in 2021] at Participant Media, when they were still around [the company was shut down in 2024]. Next year marks the 10th anniversary of the 2017 genocide.”
	

	He adds, “[It’s] a genocide that’s formally recognized as such by the United States, the EU and the British government, yet, surprisingly, no documentary feature has been produced on this subject. I’m uniquely prepared to make that film.”

	Longley doesn’t mind being an outsider. His latest, “Mohabat,” is set in Afghanistan.

	“I’m not attempting to become Afghan. I’m trying to help non-Afghans understand Afghanistan better. After fighting a war in their country for 20 years, this seems like the least we can do,” he says.

	He arrived “with a camera in my hand instead of a gun” and was treated as a guest, not an enemy.

	“I went to their country with the sincere goal of telling their stories, so I was accepted and afforded patience.

	“I cannot describe what an honor it has been for me to live and work alongside the Afghan people, who are brave and pure of heart in a way most Americans could take a good lesson from.”

	His protagonist, 12-year-old Mohabat, tries to hold his family together under Taliban rule after a U.S. drone kills his father while he’s out hunting.
	

	“This happened during the first Trump administration, when Mike Pompeo was in charge of the drone program,” says Longley.

	“During the 20-year war, such events were common and untold numbers of civilians were killed and forgotten far from the foreign journalists in Kabul. Mohabat did not want his father to be forgotten, and so he stuck with us patiently throughout two years of filming.”

	During location scouting, the team visited orphanages filled with children who had lost their parents in the war.

	“The sons of Afghan policemen martyred in Taliban suicide bombings share their bread with the sons of martyred Taliban fighters. Many of them wanted to tell their stories. That was never an issue,” he says.

	“Mohabat believed that we would do justice to the memory of his father, a poor man with a wife and seven children, who worked as a tea seller in a large market on the edge of Kabul.”

	He adds: “Elham, one of Mohabat’s friends, told us specifically that he was waiting for a foreign journalist to come and talk to them about what they had seen during the war and what they thought about it.”

	Longley is no stranger to making films “about young people and for young people,” such as “Iraq in Fragments,” “Angels Are Made of Light” and now “Mohabat.”

	“When we are children, we experience the world most directly – and for the first time. When I direct a documentary in Afghanistan, Iraq or Gaza and show it to a Western audience, I know I’m taking them to a new place. In this situation, it’s most appropriate to give them a child’s perspective because [they’re] like a child in those countries, experiencing something new.

	“I’ve included many adults in my documentaries, but most audience members never remember them after watching the film.”

	He’s influenced by Vittorio De Sica, Abbas Kiarostami, Majid Majidi, François Truffaut and other directors who “treat the lives of their child characters with great seriousness.”

	“This can also work in documentaries,” he emphasizes. Especially when working in a “restrictive space.”

	“Making a film in Afghanistan, either during the war or under the Taliban, with a child as the main protagonist doesn’t make the job more difficult; it makes it much easier. You’ll get permission to make a film about a kid a 100 times before you will get permission to make a film about an adult.”
	

	He wasn’t able to film women, however.

	“It would have caused a local scandal if one of the village women had appeared in our film. She would never have been able to live it down. The issue is not whether women can talk; it’s more that their neighbors would never stop talking about it,” he observes.

	“Plenty of Afghan women are making their own films in secret on their iPhones, so I didn’t feel it was necessary to duplicate their efforts. I’m in no position to make a film about Afghan women, and meanwhile, Afghan women filmmakers are in no position to make the kind of film we made in ‘Mohabat.’”

	He ended up joining forces with Alex Gibney, who is credited as a producer alongside Longley and Mohammad Sharif Hotak.

	“Alex saw ‘Angels Are Made of Light’ and liked it. When I asked him if he would like to produce a film with me about life in Afghanistan under the Taliban, he immediately said yes.

	“It’s been a joy working with him, mostly because he’s the best documentary producer alive and also a deeply intelligent person. This kind of collaboration and level of trust is a dream for any filmmaker.” 

	He also praises Hotak, who lived just down the road from the villages where they filmed.

	“His familiarity with the place and the people was the key to making the movie. He grew up experiencing the same realities of war as the children in the film, so he could relate to them directly.”

	Finding a personal angle is crucial for Longley, regardless of where he’s heading.

	“I see all films and media as reflecting the politics around which they were made and the politics of those who made them. Corporate news media make products that aligns with the politics of their owners and advertisers. I make films that reflect my own politics, which are pro-human and anti-war,” he notes.

	“I suspect that my films are in direct conflict with almost everything you will see on television, but I can’t say for sure – I’ve never owned a TV. I don’t care about what most of those people have to say.”

schema.headline: Oscar-Nominated Director James Longley Talks His Afghanistan Documentary ‘Mohabat’ and Why His Next Film Will Center on the Rohingya Genocide (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Forever With You’ Director Explores Grief Through a Child’s Eyes: ‘Cinema Must Be Emotionally Rooted’
description: Italian filmmaker Fabrizio Cattani brought “Forever With You,” his exploration of childhood, grief and the loss of a parent, to the Middle East for
body:
Italian filmmaker Fabrizio Cattani brought “Forever With You,” his exploration of childhood, grief and the loss of a parent, to the Middle East for the first time this week, with the film receiving a Green Carpet premiere at the 13th Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth in the UAE.




	With Italy celebrated as this year’s Country of Honor, the festival has put a spotlight on the country’s cinema. For Cattani, “Forever With You” also marks a turn toward younger audiences after previous films centered on more difficult adult subjects.
	

	Adapted from an Italian novel of the same name, “Forever With You” follows Filo, a young boy struggling to understand the death of his mother. Set in 1998 and told through flashbacks, the film turns his journey through grief into an adventure in which the people around him represent different parts of his inner world.

	“Filo, the protagonist, represents our rational part. Rullo, his friend, is the emotional part. The father is the mature part, Amelie is the childish part and Guelpho is the scary part,” Cattani tells Variety. “All these parts are inside of us. I liked using these symbols to deal with such a delicate subject as mourning.”

	For Cattani, childhood offered a way into that subject precisely because of the innocence with which Filo encounters the world.

	“He observes the world through the eyes of innocence, which we unfortunately lose when we grow up,” the director explains. “It allows him to have the strength to explore and understand the importance of small things, the things that have value.”
	

	“Childhood is very powerful because that’s where the person starts,” he adds. “Everything develops from what people experience in their childhood, what they receive in their education and what they see. We are sponges as children. What we absorb, we transmit in the later stages of our lives.”

	That perspective also places “Forever With You” within a longstanding Italian cinematic tradition of using children to explore larger social and emotional realities. Cattani points to Vittorio De Sica’s “Bicycle Thieves” as an “absolute masterpiece,” while describing his own film as distinctly Italian in its setting, dialects and other locally rooted elements.

	Shot in the autumn in Calabria, the “toe” at the end of the Italian peninsula’s boot, the film makes the region’s forests a character in their own right. Yet Cattani believes the story can travel because its central experience transcends its Italian setting. “It can open up internationally because the loss of a mother is a theme that unites the whole world,” he says.

	Cattani had already presented the film at the Locarno Film Festival, but was curious about how young audiences in the Middle East would respond to it.

	“I don’t know this culture so deeply, so I wanted to understand the reaction of the audience,” he notes. “What impressed me was seeing the kids after the screening come to thank me, congratulate me and tell me how excited they were by the film.”

	For Cattani, their reaction reinforced an idea that runs throughout his work. “The emotions connected to people very close to us, like a parent, and connected to love, unite the whole world,” he says. “For me, cinema must be emotionally rooted. A story must be emotional. Otherwise, I’m not interested.”

	Cattani also sees festivals such as SIFF as potential bridges between the Italian and Arab film industries at a moment when he says independent filmmaking in Italy faces increasing financial pressure. Beyond cultural exchange, he hopes stronger ties could eventually extend to production and financing.

	His next film, however, takes him back toward an adult protagonist. Set around the marble quarries of Carrara in Tuscany, where Cattani grew up, the project centers on the “medico condotto,” the village doctors who once served small Italian communities and whose role disappeared following changes to the country’s health system.
	

	But Cattani is already developing another project that would bring him back to young protagonists. “Young Rebels” is based on the true story of a group of young scouts who defied a fascist ban on Catholic associations and continued their activities in secret, helping thousands of people targeted by the regime escape across the mountains into Switzerland.

	“It is a film that talks about freedom,” Cattani says. “They rebelled against this imposition and decided to embrace freedom and help people who were being persecuted.”

	After “Forever With You,” Cattani plans to continue exploring stories centered on childhood.

	“I think children have a lot to say and a lot to give to adults,” he argues. “Today’s young people have an incredible maturity.”

schema.headline: ‘Forever With You’ Director Explores Grief Through a Child’s Eyes: ‘Cinema Must Be Emotionally Rooted’

title: ’14th’ Director Ava DuVernay on Midterm Elections: ‘Either Way We’re in Trouble’
description:
Oscar-nominated filmmaker Ava DuVernay is warning that the midterm elections aren’t looking great for the U.S. — no matter what the outcome.

	“I t
body:
Oscar-nominated filmmaker Ava DuVernay is warning that the midterm elections aren’t looking great for the U.S. — no matter what the outcome.

	“I think either way we’re in trouble,” DuVernay told me at the Airbnb.org Gala last week. “If the Democrats pull it out, I think you’re going to see an outsized reaction from the administration and I think if they don’t, you’re going to see an outsized reaction from the administration.”
	

	DuVernay’s latest documentary, “14th,” has earned critical acclaim and award season buzz. The film takes a look at the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which established birthright citizenship, due process and equal protection under the law.

	“Folks need to really understand what it means to be a citizen, what it means to fight and to really know your rights,” DuVernay said.

	With just two days to go until Election Day, more than 43 million Americans have already voted early in person or returned mail ballots, The Associated Press reported on Oct. 30. According to the latest national congressional ballot average shows Democrats still lead Republicans by 8.2 percentage points. Democrats lead by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, according to RealClearPolling. It is widely predicted that the Democrats will regain control of the House of Representatives. The Dems have the chance to flip the Senate as well, but the races are too tight to call anything as definitive as the House.

	Asked what her next doc till tackle, DuVernay said, “There’s so much going on. There’s no lack of material or things to look at or advocate for, so we all need to keep our eye on the ball and keep pushing forward.”

title: Horrifying Audio of Palm Beach Plane Flight Moments Before Crash Revealed
description:
Palm Beach Plane Crash
                          Chilling Audio Revealed
body:
Palm Beach Plane Crash
                          Chilling Audio Revealed
                          'We're Out of Time'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 1, 2026
                            2:11 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 1, 2026
                                3:04 PM PST
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Audio between air traffic control and a Learjet flight in the moments before it crashed show the plane's crew scrambling to respond as they plummeted in a nose dive.
      
    
            In audio first reported by the California Post, one female crew member yelled ... "Holy f***, we're out of time."
      

            The audio begins with the flight crew telling air traffic controllers that they had experienced moderate turbulence and were dealing with ice.
      
    
            After experiencing precipitation ... the flight said they were going to climb.
      
    
            Then in a mayday call ... the flight crew alerted air traffic control that they were descending 10,000 feet per minute.
      
    
            The call then became more frantic ... as the crew shared that they were now descending 20,000 feet per minute. Flight data would eventually show them descending 32,000 feet per minute -- roughly 360 MPH.
      
    
            Eventually, the crew member tells air traffic controllers ... "We're going to crash into the ground."
      
    
            After the crew member let out a high pitch scream, the air traffic controller then responded ... "I'm here with you, talk with me."
      
    
            The crew member then responded that the aircraft was banking at 60 degrees ... before their audio cut out.
      
    
            We reported earlier ... all 9 people aboard died after the plane crashed near the Cresthaven neighborhood close to Greenacres, Florida, just miles away from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago.
